ai.title: Intracerebral Haemorrhage
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Bleeding within brain parenchyma, often due to hypertension or vascular malformations, presents with sudden focal deficits. Rapid assessment, imaging, and blood pressure control are life‑saving.

b: Hypertension is the leading cause; others include amyloid angiopathy, vascular malformations, anticoagulation, trauma, and infections.
sections.p: Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) is bleeding into the brain tissue itself, distinct from subarachnoid or intraventricular haemorrhage. It is a medical emergency with high mortality.

ICH severity is graded by the World Federation of Neurological Surgeons (WFNS) scale and the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). Early CT is diagnostic. Blood pressure should be lowered to 140–160 mmHg systolic if GCS ≥ 9.

t.b: Elevated INR >1.5 or aPTT >1.5× normal indicates anticoagulation‑related bleed; reversal is urgent.
Hyperglycaemia >180 mg/dL worsens outcome; treat to 140–180 mg/dL.

sections.p: Patients present with sudden headache, weakness, speech disturbance, or altered consciousness. In low‑resource settings, delays in imaging and blood pressure control increase mortality.

t.b: Detects papilledema indicating raised intracranial pressure; urgent decompression may be needed.
Rule out hypoglycaemia as a reversible cause of altered sensorium.

sections.p: Examiners test your ability to triage, interpret imaging, and manage blood pressure. They also probe knowledge of contraindications to anticoagulation reversal.

t.b: A GCS <9 warrants immediate airway protection and possible surgical intervention.

sections.p: Over‑aggressive lowering of blood pressure can precipitate cerebral hypoperfusion. Failure to recognise anticoagulation reversal needs leads to re‑bleeding.

t.b: Failure to give vitamin K or PCC in warfarin‑related ICH can worsen outcomes.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control blood pressure, reverse anticoagulation if indicated, and monitor for raised intracranial pressure.

t.b: Rapidly restores clotting factors; preferred over fresh frozen plasma.
Used for cerebral oedema; give 0.25–0.5 g/kg if ICP >20 mmHg.

sections.p: Intracerebral haemorrhage can be mistaken for subarachnoid haemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or severe migraine with aura.
Normal CT in the first hour does not exclude haemorrhage; repeat imaging if clinical suspicion remains high.
Any sudden neurological deficit, loss of consciousness, or severe headache warrants urgent transfer to a facility with CT and neurosurgical capability.

t.a: What is the most common cause of ICH in East Africa?
t.b: Hypertension, often uncontrolled due to limited access to care.
Severe cerebral malaria can lead to haemorrhagic lesions, but true ICH is rare.

t.a: Is anticoagulation always contraindicated in ICH?
t.b: No, but it must be reversed urgently if the patient is on warfarin or DOACs.

t.a: Why is mannitol avoided in patients with uncontrolled hypertension?
t.b: It can worsen cerebral oedema and increase intracranial pressure if BP is not controlled.

t.a: What distinguishes ICH from subarachnoid haemorrhage on CT?
t.b: ICH shows a hyperdense area within brain parenchyma; SAH shows hyperdensity in the cisterns and sulci.

t.a: Why should you not give aspirin to a patient with ICH?
t.b: Aspirin impairs platelet function and increases risk of re‑bleeding.
